4v4-attack-losange.title: 4v4 · Diamond attack
4v4-attack-losange.shortDescription: Canonical diamond: setter at P3 + 2 wings on the 3 m line + back. Reception → zone-4 attack.

s1.title: 1. Diamond formation
s1.description: Canonical layout: setter AT THE CENTER of the net (P3) + 2 wings on the 3 m line + back deep.

s2.title: 2. Serve + back-court reception
s2.description: The lone back moves forward and bumps. High trajectory toward the setter at the net.

s3.title: 3. Set + approach + coverage
s3.description: R4 chains his approach toward zone 4. Setter, A2 and A close into a triangle for coverage. Opposing block slides toward the hitter.

s4.title: 4. Cross-court spike + single block
s4.description: Powerful spike. Against a single block the angle is wide: the hitter can aim long cross-court or short line.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing cross defender dives on the long cross-court — arrives a touch too late, the ball has already hit the floor.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to diamond
s6.description: Everyone resumes their position in the diamond for the next rally. The setter returns to the center of the net.

keyPoints: Canonical diamond = the most common 4v4 formation.
"Center setter" variant: setter at P3, distributes to the left or to the right.
Standard single opposing block in 4v4: wide attack angle.
Limited coverage: 3 players around the hitter.
commonMistakes: Setter who also receives → impossible to set behind.
Wings too deep → difficult set for the center setter.
Back too deep → no coverage of short block returns.

4v4-attack-penetrant.title: 4v4 · Penetrating setter
4v4-attack-penetrant.shortDescription: Simplified 3-1 system: single setter in P1 penetrates to zone 2, freeing 3 front-row hitters.

s1.title: 1. 3-1 configuration
s1.description: Single setter in P1 (back-row). 3 hitters in front at P2, P3, P4. No libero: the receiver chains his approach.

s2.title: 2. Serve + reception + penetration
s2.description: The left wing bumps the reception. The setter simultaneously launches his penetration from P1 toward zone 2.

s3.title: 3. Set + R4 approach
s3.description: High set toward the left wing after R4's reception run. The opposing block slides toward him.

s4.title: 4. Cross-court spike + single block
s4.description: Powerful long cross-court spike. With only 3 coverers, they form a short triangle around the hitter.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing cross defender dives on the long cross-court — arrives 0.1 s too late on impact.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: The setter returns to back-row P1, R4 returns to zone 4. The penetration must be anticipated from the next serve onward.

keyPoints: 3-1 system = the 4v4 equivalent of the 5-1. 1 dedicated penetrating setter.
Advantage: 3 hitters in front at all times, like in 6v6.
Drawback: requires very clean reception since the setter is not at the net.
No libero: the receiver also chains his attack approach.
commonMistakes: Penetration too late → another player has to make the set.
Reception too short → setter arrives too far from the net.
Coverage forgotten — opposing block-out = point.

4v4-attack-square.title: 4v4 · Box attack
4v4-attack-square.shortDescription: Box formation (2 front / 2 back): 2 blockers + 2 balanced defenders.

s1.title: 1. Box configuration
s1.description: 2 players at the net (P2 and P4), 2 players at the back. Balanced coverage of the court front and back.

s2.title: 2. Serve + high reception
s2.description: The left back bumps a lofted pass to the setter-hitter in zone 2.

s3.title: 3. Set to the wing + approach
s3.description: The setter distributes to the hitter in zone 4. No middle option (no specialized middle). The double block slides toward the hitter.

s4.title: 4. Spike against a double block
s4.description: The hitter must choose: short line, long cross-court or tip into the open lane. Double block (vs single block in the diamond) — defense made tougher offensively.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing cross defender dives on the long cross-court. With only 2 players on the floor, the zone is vulnerable.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: Everyone resumes the box for the next rally. This formation suits teams with 2 strong blockers and 2 strong defenders.

keyPoints: Box formation: balance between attack/defense, 2 front zones + 2 back zones.
Allows a double block (vs single block of the diamond) — better defense at the net.
But only 2 players on the floor → vulnerable to long cross-courts.
Good for teams with 2 strong blockers and 2 strong defenders.
commonMistakes: Net players too far from the center → easy opposing block.
Backs frozen deep → no short coverage.
Confusion over who sets: the setter-hitter must always be in front.

5v5-attack-pentagon.title: 5v5 · Pentagon attack
5v5-attack-pentagon.shortDescription: 5v5 format: 1 single setter + 1 middle + 2 wings + 1 back. Zone-4 attack.

s1.title: 1. Offensive pentagon
s1.description: 5 players in a pentagon: 3 in front (R4, C, P) + 2 in the back. Regular court coverage. No libero, all backs receive.

s2.title: 2. Serve + back reception
s2.description: The left back takes the first ball. Without a libero, the most reliable back in reception takes it.

s3.title: 3. Set + approach
s3.description: The setter, already at the net, easily distributes to zone 4. No penetration in 5v5 — he is in P2. R4 starts his approach.

s4.title: 4. Wing attack + double block
s4.description: The left wing finishes long cross-court. The opposing block also pentagons up: 2 blockers on the wing.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing cross defender dives on the cross-court. Floor defense is rarer with a single back per channel.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: Everyone resumes the pentagon. Without a libero, rotating the backs is essential to spread the reception load.

keyPoints: 5v5 = hybrid format (training, missing players). No official FFVB rules.
Pentagon: 1 player per key zone, regular coverage of the whole court.
4-1 system = equivalent of the 5-1 but with one less hitter.
Recommendation: keep the 6v6 5-1 system by removing one non-setter back.
commonMistakes: No libero in 5v5 → all backs must be able to receive.
Trying to triple-block → only 2 floor defenders left.
Forgetting attack coverage → one less player in coverage.

6v6-attack-4-2.title: Attack · 4-2 system
6v6-attack-4-2.shortDescription: Beginner 4-2 system: fixed front-row setter in zone 2, 2 hitters available.

s1.title: 1. 4-2 configuration
s1.description: 2 setters in diagonal opposition (P2 and P5). The front-row setter (P1) always makes the 2nd touch. W reception with C2 in the center.

s2.title: 2. Serve + central reception
s2.description: The back middle takes the first touch in a classic W reception. High trajectory to the front setter in P2.

s3.title: 3. Direct set + approach
s3.description: The front setter only needs to distribute: no penetration, no switch. He sends a high set to the OH in zone 4. Double block on the wing.

s4.title: 4. Wing attack + double block
s4.description: The OH attacks in zone 4. No middle option since the middle received. Spike on the long cross-court against a double block.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing cross defender dives cross-court to try to recover the ball.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: Everyone resumes their position. The 4-2 remains the simplest system: no switch required.

keyPoints: 4-2: 2 setters + 2 middles + 2 outsides. Always 2 hitters in front.
The front setter (in P2 or P3 depending on the variant) systematically makes the 2nd touch.
No penetration, no switch: the easiest system to learn.
Ideal for U13/U15 or adult beginners. Promotes learning rotations.
commonMistakes: Front setter who also receives → impossible to make the 2nd touch.
Back setter wanting to set → front-setter rule not respected.
Middle who does not commit → easy double block.

6v6-attack-5-1-p1.title: Attack · 5-1 P1 rotation
6v6-attack-5-1-p1.shortDescription: 3-receiver reception → setter penetrates from P1 → zone-4 attack by the OH.

s1.title: 1. Reception formation
s1.description: Our team is in a 3-receiver formation: libero (P5), OH in P6 and OH in P4 pulled back on the 3 m line. Middle and opposite are out at the net. The setter waits in P1 to penetrate as soon as the serve is struck.

s2.title: 2. Serve + reception
s2.description: Opposing lofted serve to the OH in P6 who bumps it. In parallel, the setter triggers his penetration from P1 toward zone 2-3.

s3.title: 3. High set + approach
s3.description: The ball rises to the setter who has arrived at the net. He delivers a lofted set to zone 4 where the OH has already started his approach. Coverage forms around him.

s4.title: 4. Spike + double block
s4.description: The OH lifts off and hits long cross-court toward the opponent's zone 6. The two opposing blockers jump in parallel to close cross-court and line.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing libero dives toward zone 6 to try a desperate bump. The opposing setter moves toward zone 2 to relay if defense touches the ball.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: The whole team resumes its reception position for the next serve. This placement determines the quality of the next attack.

keyPoints: 3-receiver reception: libero + 2 OHs take the full width of the court.
The setter penetrates from P1 toward zone 2-3 as soon as the serve is struck.
The OH attacker slides on the 3 m line during reception to prepare his approach.
5-player coverage (3 close + 2 far) in low position around the hitter.
commonMistakes: Setter penetrating too late → forced jump set by another player.
OH attacker triggering his approach too early → arrives under the ball instead of committing.
Coverage forgotten → successful opposing block = point lost directly.

6v6-attack-5-1-p2.title: Attack · 5-1 P2 rotation
6v6-attack-5-1-p2.shortDescription: Setter already at the net in P2: 2 hitters in front + opposite attacks in 4 exceptionally.

s1.title: 1. Opposing serve
s1.description: Serve toward zone 5-6. The libero calls and prepares to bump. The setter already waits at the net in P2.

s2.title: 2. Serve + libero reception
s2.description: Lofted serve to zone 6. The libero steps in and bumps precisely to the setter target (zone 2).

s3.title: 3. Set to the opposite + approach
s3.description: The setter, already in P2, exceptionally distributes to zone 4 where the opposite starts his approach. The opposing block regroups in the center.

s4.title: 4. Spike + double block
s4.description: The opposite lifts off on the left and hits long cross-court. A rare configuration but unavoidable in P2 — the setter stays in place.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing cross defender dives on the long cross-court to try a desperate bump save.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: Everyone resumes their reception position. The P2 rotation remains the most offensively limited: only 2 hitters in front.

keyPoints: P2 rotation = the most offensively limited (only 2 hitters in front).
Setter already in place: zero penetration, easy distribution.
The opposite exceptionally attacks on the left (zone 4) to free the setter.
Prioritize the wings and OH back-row attacks as options.
commonMistakes: Setter trying to jump-set in 2 when he's already there → difficult 2nd touch.
Opposite hesitating between 2 and 4 → opposing block in place.
Middles not committing → easy double block for the opponent.

6v6-attack-5-1-p3.title: Attack · 5-1 P3 rotation (pipe)
6v6-attack-5-1-p3.shortDescription: Setter at P3 switches toward 2-3 → pipe by the back-row OH in zone 6.

s1.title: 1. Reception formation
s1.description: Serve expected on the right side. The OH in P1 takes the reception. The setter in P3 is ready to switch toward 2-3 as soon as the serve is struck.

s2.title: 2. Serve + reception
s2.description: Lofted serve to zone 1. The OH in P1 bumps to the target. The setter starts his switch toward 2-3.

s3.title: 3. Pipe set + approach
s3.description: The setter sends a flat set to zone 6: fast trajectory 2 m from the net. The opposite launches his approach behind the 3 m line for the pipe.

s4.title: 4. Pipe + double block
s4.description: Powerful hit in the center from the back court. The wing double block cannot screen at the center — a key option of the modern 5-1.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing central defender dives at the core to try to catch the pipe — the ball arrives fast, little time to react.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: The whole team resumes its reception position. The middle must stay ready to switch to the center of the net for the next sequence.

keyPoints: The pipe is the 4th offensive option on top of the 3 attacks at the net.
The middle switches to the center of the net while the setter slides to 2-3.
Pipe trajectory: flat, 2 m from the net, take-off behind the 3 m line.
Very effective against a block that focuses on the wings.
commonMistakes: Pipe too high → opposing block has time to recover to the center.
Back-row OH taking off in the front zone → back-row attack fault.
Middle switching too late → zone 3 blocked.

6v6-attack-5-1-p4.title: Attack · 5-1 P4 rotation
6v6-attack-5-1-p4.shortDescription: Front-row setter at P4 switches to the right; OH* attacks in 4, middle in 3, opposite back-row in 1.

s1.title: 1. P4 configuration + offset
s1.description: Setter in zone 4, OH* in zone 2 — crossed placement. Setter and middle shift left to free the reception zone for the libero.

s2.title: 2. Serve + libero reception
s2.description: The serve targets zone 6. The libero steps in and bumps to the classic target (between P2 and P3).

s3.title: 3. Setter↔OH* switch + high set
s3.description: Essential crossover: the setter leaves P4 toward 2-3, the OH* leaves P2 toward 4 to attack. Lofted set to the left wing.

s4.title: 4. Wing attack + double block
s4.description: Long cross-court spike. With a front-row setter (small at the block), the attack must finish quickly. Double block shifted toward the wing.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing diagonal defender dives on the long trajectory to try a desperate bump.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: Everyone resumes their initial position. The setter/middle left offset is kept for the next serve.

keyPoints: P4 rotation = front-row setter. Setter↔OH* switch mandatory.
2 hitters in front: OH* in 4, middle in 3. Pipe or back-row opposite as options.
The setter and middle shift left at the serve to free zone 6.
The opposite (in P1) does not receive and stays ready for a back-row attack.
commonMistakes: Switch forgotten → the OH* stays on the right, hitter in poor position.
Setter and middle too far right at the serve → reception conflict in zone 6.
Opposing block not committed by the middle → easy double block on the left wing.

6v6-attack-5-1-p5.title: Attack · 5-1 P5 rotation
6v6-attack-5-1-p5.shortDescription: Long penetration from P5. C/OH switch. Set to the opposite in zone 2.

s1.title: 1. Reception formation
s1.description: Setter in back-left P5, as far from the net as possible. C in P4 and OH in P3 will switch as soon as the serve is struck.

s2.title: 2. Serve + reception + C↔OH switch
s2.description: The serve targets zone 1 where the OH receives. Simultaneously, the middle slides to the center and the attacking OH takes zone 4.

s3.title: 3. Long penetration + set in zone 2
s3.description: The setter crosses the whole court from P5 — the longest penetration. He distributes short to the opposite in zone 2. The opposing block slides right to close.

s4.title: 4. Cross-court spike + double block
s4.description: The opposite lifts off in zone 2 and hits long cross-court. A classic combination on this rotation. The double block is in place on the right.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The opposing diagonal defender dives into zone 5 to try to catch the long ball.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: The whole team resumes its reception position. The middle returns to P4, the OH to P3, the setter to P5.

keyPoints: P5 = the longest penetration. Requires perfect reception.
The middle and the OH switch as soon as the serve is struck to place C in zone 3.
The opposite in zone 2 is the most accessible target for the setter.
Pipe possible as an option if the set is flat and fast.
commonMistakes: Too flat a set during an ongoing penetration → setter under the ball.
Late C↔OH switch → middle in zone 4 = useless at the block.
Short reception → setter arrives too far from the net.

6v6-attack-5-1-p6.title: Attack · 5-1 P6 rotation (quick)
6v6-attack-5-1-p6.shortDescription: Medium penetration from P6 → fast central attack by the middle.

s1.title: 1. Reception formation
s1.description: Serve expected on the left side. The libero takes his channel. The opposite at P3 will switch to P2, the middle at P2 will slide to the center of the net.

s2.title: 2. Serve + reception + Opp↔C switch
s2.description: Lofted serve to zone 5. The libero receives. The opposite slides to zone 2 and the middle takes the center of the net to prepare the quick.

s3.title: 3. Medium penetration
s3.description: The setter crosses from P6 to zone 2-3 (medium path, shorter than P5). The middle starts to load for tempo 1.

s4.title: 4. Pre-jump + fast flat set
s4.description: The middle takes off ALREADY before the set — that's tempo 1. The setter sends a fast ball at 1 m, just in front of him. The middle is already airborne.

s5.title: 5. Center hit + block too late
s5.description: Fast central hit that surprises the opposing block before it's in place. The opposing blockers jump just after — too late.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: The middle returns to the center, everyone resumes the reception formation. The fast central is the signature combination of this rotation.

keyPoints: P6 = medium penetration. Ideal for fast combinations.
Tempo 1: middle already in the air when the setter touches the ball.
The middle commits the opposing central block: frees the wings for the OHs.
Systematic Opp↔C switch to place the middle back at the center.
commonMistakes: Middle taking off too late → ball passes over his hand.
Set too high for tempo 1 → opposing block in place.
Opposite who does not switch → middle stuck in zone 2.

6v6-attack-6-2.title: Attack · 6-2 system
6v6-attack-6-2.shortDescription: 6-2 system: back-row setter penetrates, 3 hitters in front at all times.

s1.title: 1. 6-2 configuration
s1.description: 2 versatile setters: the front one attacks (setter-hitter), the back one distributes (and penetrates). 3 hitters in front at all times.

s2.title: 2. Serve + back-middle reception
s2.description: Classic central reception by C2. The setter triggers his penetration from P1 toward zone 2-3.

s3.title: 3. Set in zone 2 + approach
s3.description: Distribution to the setter-hitter in zone 2. Maximum variety: 3 offensive threats in front. Double block shifted to the right.

s4.title: 4. Cross-court attack + double block
s4.description: The setter-hitter hits long cross-court. The 6-2 always guarantees 3 offensive threats — the opposing block cannot anticipate.

s5.title: 5. Opposing dig
s5.description: The cross defender dives on the long trajectory on the opponent's left side — a desperate save attempt.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to formation
s6.description: The whole team resumes its position. The setter-hitter stays in front, the setter returns to P1.

keyPoints: 6-2: 2 versatile setters in diagonal opposition.
Always 3 hitters in front (the front setter attacks, the back setter distributes).
Systematic penetration, like in 5-1, but with 2 alternating distributors.
Excellent for developing versatility before switching to a 5-1.
commonMistakes: Style difference between the 2 setters → inconsistent distribution.
Front setter not showing up for the attack → only 2 options.
Penetration too late → another player has to make the set.

4v4-defense-block-1.title: 4v4 · System A defense (1 blocker + 3 defenders)
4v4-defense-block-1.shortDescription: System A in 4v4 (diamond formation): 1 solo blocker + tip + cross + line. The most common configuration.

s1.title: 1. Diamond base + read
s1.description: With 4 players each defender is crucial. Our middle prepares to block solo. Mandatory read of the opposing set.

s2.title: 2. High set to opposing Z2
s2.description: Distribution to their right wing. The attack arrives on our front-LEFT corner. The middle must slide to the left side.

s3.title: 3. Solo central block + line/cross signal
s3.description: The middle slides left and blocks alone. Mandatory signal (line or cross-court) to orient the 3 defenders. Without a signal, they don't know what to cover.

s4.title: 4. Long cross-court spike + block
s4.description: The hitter strikes long cross-court. The solo block closes the line, signal announced beforehand.

s5.title: 5. Recovery by the lone back
s5.description: The P1 back defends in his axis — his read must be perfect, no other back to compensate. High bump to the target.

s6.title: 6. RESET — diamond formation
s6.description: Back to the diamond formation. Coverage will adapt to the next attack zone from the next read on.

keyPoints: System A (1 blocker + 3 defenders): the most common configuration in indoor 4v4.
Line/cross blocker signal mandatory — without it, the 3 defenders don't know what to cover.
Key distances: blocker 0.3 m from the net; deep defenders 7-7.5 m; tip/behind-block 3.5-4 m.
Each defender covers ~30-40 m² (vs 20 m² in 6v6) → anticipation = skill #1.
Double block (system B) reserved for big hitters: leaves only 2 deep defenders.
commonMistakes: Isolated blocker with no tip coverage: the 3 defenders all go deep, leaving the 3-5 m zone empty.
2 defenders in a straight line: side by side at the same depth → the cut shot lands between them.
No signal between blocker and defenders (line vs cross-court).
Tip defender too far from the net: drops back with the others and can no longer cover short tips.
Setter running to his target before the ball is defended → defensive hole.

4v4-defense-vs-z2.title: 4v4 · Z2 defense
4v4-defense-vs-z2.shortDescription: Mirror of system A: 1 blocker + 3 defenders against opposing Z2 attack (their right → arrives on our left).

s1.title: 1. Read opposing Z2 attack
s1.description: Opposing attack from their zone 2 (their right) → arrives on our front-LEFT corner. The middle will need to slide to the left side to block.

s2.title: 2. High set to opposing Z2
s2.description: Distribution to their right wing. The defense triggers its mirror adjustment.

s3.title: 3. Solo central block on the left side
s3.description: The middle slides to the left side and blocks alone. Line/cross signal mandatory. R4 (left wing) stays off-blocker at 2.5 m, A2 (right wing) defends the long cross-court.

s4.title: 4. Diagonal spike + solo block
s4.description: The hitter strikes long cross-court. The solo block covers the signaled line.

s5.title: 5. Recovery by the lone back
s5.description: The P1 back (slightly shifted to the ball side) defends with a bump. His read compensates for the absence of other backs.

s6.title: 6. RESET — diamond formation
s6.description: Back to diamond formation. The middle returns to the center, ready to slide again if the opponent switches sides.

keyPoints: Perfect mirror of Z4 in 4v4: system A (1 blocker + 3 defenders).
P3 solo blocker on the left side, line/cross signal mandatory.
P4 (left wing) as off-blocker 3.5-4 m from the net — short coverage and tips.
P2 (right wing) defends the short cross-court (~7 m, straight line).
The lone P1 back defends the long cross-court.
commonMistakes: Left wing P4 blocking with the middle → off-blocker missing on the left side.
Lone back too far forward → deep cross-court ball not covered.
Blocker with no signal → the 3 defenders don't know what to cover.
P2 too far from the net → does not cover the short cross-court.

4v4-defense-vs-z3.title: 4v4 · Z3 defense (central quick)
4v4-defense-vs-z3.shortDescription: Opposing fast central attack in 4v4: read block-of-1 + 3 defenders. The hardest configuration to defend.

s1.title: 1. Read opposing quick
s1.description: In 4v4 the central quick (tempo 1) is the most dangerous attack since only 1 blocker is available. The lone back already scans the deep axis.

s2.title: 2. Fast central set
s2.description: The setter flat-sets to the middle who has already started his approach. Our wings drop to mid-court to cover the cross-courts.

s3.title: 3. Block-of-1 (read) + fast spike
s3.description: The middle alone jumps on a READ — no commitment possible with a defensive middle. The opposing middle hits straight down the axis.

s4.title: 4. Defensive pivot: the lone back
s4.description: The P1 back defends the powerful ball straight on axis — he plays the role of Z6 of 6v6. His read must be PERFECT.

s5.title: 5. RESET — diamond formation
s5.description: Back to 4v4 base. The middle drops back at the net, the back resumes his axial position.

keyPoints: The 4v4 doc confirms it: the central quick is A REAL WEAKNESS of 4v4 (only 1 blocker).
Block-of-1 on READ: no commitment possible with a defensive middle.
The 2 wings cover the 2 short cross-courts at mid-court (~3.5-4 m from the net).
The lone back is the defensive pivot — he plays the role of Z6 of 6v6 on the central axis.
Anticipation = skill #1: with ~40 m² to cover, a read error is unrecoverable.
commonMistakes: Double block on a quick → only 2 floor defenders, cross-courts wide open.
Back moving forward too early → deep ball lands behind him.
Wings staying at the net without blocking → holes on the 3 m line behind the block.
Read of the opposing middle too late → we absorb the attack without moving.

5v5-defense-vs-z2.title: 5v5 · Z2 defense
5v5-defense-vs-z2.shortDescription: Perfect mirror of Z4. 2-1-2 system against opposing Z2 attack (their right → arrives on our left).

s1.title: 1. Read opposing Z2 attack
s1.description: Opposing attack from their zone 2 (their right) → arrives on our front-LEFT corner. Perfect mirror of Z4.

s2.title: 2. High set to opposing Z2
s2.description: Distribution to their right wing. The attack arrives on our front-LEFT corner.

s3.title: 3. Mirror double block (OH + middle)
s3.description: OH blocker line + middle cross-court on the left side. Opposite (P2) drops off as off-blocker on the right. Libero defends the line in the block shadow, setter defends the long cross-court.

s4.title: 4. Spike + double block
s4.description: The opposing right wing hits long cross-court. OH + middle jump.

s5.title: 5. Setter defense — complex transition
s5.description: The setter is on the long cross-court trajectory. Defensive bump — since he's the primary defender, the opposite must take the 2nd touch.

s6.title: 6. RESET
s6.description: Back to 5v5 base. Mandatory communication between setter and opposite for the next sequence.

keyPoints: Perfect mirror of Z4 in 5v5: 2-1-2 system (double block + off-blocker + 2 defenders).
Double block: OH (P4) blocker line + middle (P3) closes the cross-court.
The opposite (P2) becomes off-blocker on the right side, drops off on the 3 m line.
The back-row setter (P1) defends the long cross-court.
If the setter defends → 2nd touch by the opposite (back-up setter) is mandatory.
commonMistakes: Opposite blocking from Z2 → off-blocker missing on the right side.
Setter who defends AND wants to relay → confusion on the 2nd touch.
Libero misplaced on Z2 (defends the LINE here, not the long cross-court).
No communication between setter and opposite.

5v5-defense-vs-z3.title: 5v5 · Z3 defense (quick / tempo 1)
5v5-defense-vs-z3.shortDescription: Block-of-1 (middle) on opposing central quick attack in 5v5 — partial axial coverage.

s1.title: 1. Read opposing quick
s1.description: Flat distribution imminent toward the middle. 0.3-0.5 s between set and hit — our middle scans his counterpart, already on the move.

s2.title: 2. Flat set + wings as off-blockers
s2.description: The opposing setter flat-sets the middle. Our wings drop to 1.5 m from the net on the attack line to cover lateral deflections.

s3.title: 3. Block-of-1 (read) + fast spike
s3.description: Our middle alone jumps on a read. The opposing middle hits short cross-court — angles are short compared to a high set.

s4.title: 4. Libero defense
s4.description: The libero (pulled up to 5 m since angles are short) defends with a bump in his left channel. High trajectory to the target — the setter will return to the net.

s5.title: 5. RESET
s5.description: Back to 5v5 base after the sequence. The middle and wings realign.

keyPoints: Block-of-1 (P3 middle) on read — no commit possible on a quick.
Wings (P4 + P2) 2 m from the net on the attack line: cover block deflections.
With only 2 deep defenders (P5 + P1), AXIAL deep coverage is partial.
Z1 and Z5 ADVANCE 1 m (~7 m from the net) because angles are shorter on a quick.
"Stopped on contact": everyone stopped at the exact moment of the hit.
commonMistakes: Double block on a quick → too late, and leaves only 1 floor defender.
Defenders frozen at the back (8 m+) → fast ball lands before they move.
"False stepping" (first step backwards) → time lost on tempo 1.
Off-blockers staying at the net → don't cover deflections.

5v5-defense-vs-z4.title: 5v5 · Z4 defense
5v5-defense-vs-z4.shortDescription: 2-1-2 system against opposing Z4 attack (their left → arrives on our right): double block + off-blocker + 2 defenders.

s1.title: 1. Read opposing Z4 attack
s1.description: Opposing attack from their zone 4 (their left) → arrives on our front-RIGHT corner. Sequential read "ball → setter → ball → hitter".

s2.title: 2. High set to opposing Z4
s2.description: Standard distribution from their setter to the left wing. Our front line identifies the attack zone.

s3.title: 3. Double block + OH off-blocker
s3.description: Opposite (P2) + middle (P3) go up to block on the right side. OH drops off at 1.5 m from the net as off-blocker. Libero in the long cross-court, setter on the straight line — each covers ~30 m².

s4.title: 4. Long cross-court spike + block
s4.description: The hitter strikes long cross-court (statistically the most frequent trajectory). Opposite + middle jump.

s5.title: 5. Libero defense
s5.description: The libero is on the main trajectory. High bump to the target — transition to counter-attack.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to 2-1-2 base
s6.description: Switch to base formation. The setter returns to his zone 1, defense reorganizes for the next sequence.

keyPoints: 2-1-2 system: 2 blockers + 1 off-blocker (tip coverer) + 2 deep defenders.
Recommendation: keep the 6v6 5-1 by removing one non-setter back (3F-2B configuration).
Off-blocker 2-2.5 m from the net, 1 m from the line — covers the 3 m zone behind the block.
Critical read: ~30 m² per defender (vs 20 m² in 6v6), reduced initial positional safety.
"Stopped on contact": stopped and balanced at the exact moment of the hit.
commonMistakes: Triple block → only 1 floor defender = guaranteed point.
Off-blocker staying at the net → 3 m zone behind the block uncovered.
No priority hierarchy between the 2 deep defenders → 2 players on the same ball.
Mechanically reproducing 6v6 without adapting zones (the libero must cover wider here).

6v6-attack-coverage.title: Coverage · 5-1 attack
6v6-attack-coverage.shortDescription: 5-player coverage on a zone-4 attack: 2 arcs (3 close + 2 far) to dig a potential block-out.

s1.title: 1. Preparing the Z4 attack
s1.description: Our OH is in his approach, about to take off. Even before the hit, coverage organizes: it's anticipation that saves a block-out, not reaction.

s2.title: 2. First arc (3 close players)
s2.description: Setter + middle + libero form a half-circle 1-1.5 m from the hitter, VERY low position, arms extended forward, ready to short-bump.

s3.title: 3. Spike + opposing double block
s3.description: Our OH lifts off and hits cross-court. The two opposing blockers jump in parallel to close the trajectory — coverage is already frozen, waiting.

s4.title: 4. Block-out: the ball comes back
s4.description: The opposing block touches the ball which ricochets into our court 1.5 m from the hitter. Without coverage, that's a lost point — here, the setter is exactly at the landing spot.

s5.title: 5. Recovery by the setter (1st support)
s5.description: The setter (1st close support) digs the ball with a bump 1 m from the hitter. It's HIS responsibility after a set to zone 4 — non-negotiable rule.

s6.title: 6. New attack possible
s6.description: The save allows a new ball back at the net. Without 5-player coverage = point lost directly on the block-out.

keyPoints: 5-player coverage = elite-level standard. 3-2 layout (3 close + 2 far).
The setter is ALWAYS the 1st close support, 1-1.5 m from the hitter.
VERY low position for the 3 close players, arms extended forward.
Without coverage, a successful opposing block = point lost directly.
Anticipation outweighs reaction: coverage organizes BEFORE the hit.
commonMistakes: No coverage → opposing block = point.
Setter staying at the net after his set → 1st support missing.
Coverers standing or too far → short balls not recovered.
Only 2 or 3 coverers instead of 5 → long block-outs lost.

6v6-defense-6-front.title: Defense · man-up (2-1-3)
6v6-defense-6-front.shortDescription: Man-up system (2-1-3, formerly "W defense"): a defender pulled up behind the block for short tips.

s1.title: 1. Man-up base
s1.description: The opponent is known for tipping — tactical choice of the man-up. The OH (in P6) is already pulled up to 2.5 m, ready to move up behind the block.

s2.title: 2. Opposing high set to Z4
s2.description: Standard distribution to opposing Z4. The defense recognizes the configuration and sets up.

s3.title: 3. Player up behind the block
s3.description: Key difference of the man-up: R4b moves up to 2.5 m from the net, in the block shadow. Libero and setter drop back to 6 m to compensate. Standard double block (opposite + middle).

s4.title: 4. Opposing jump tip
s4.description: The hitter chooses to tip rather than spike. The ball lands just behind the block — exactly where the up-player is.

s5.title: 5. Short recovery by the up-player
s5.description: The up-player is exactly where the ball falls. Precise bump to the opposite to relay a jump 2nd touch.

s6.title: 6. RESET — man-up base
s6.description: Back to 2-1-3 base position. R4b repositioned at 2.5 m, libero and setter deep.

keyPoints: Man-up = 2-1-3 (Keller / USAV) — formerly "red defense".
⚠ DO NOT confuse with "W-formation" which is a RECEPTION formation, not a defensive system.
Exceptional coverage of tips, roll shots and "junk" balls behind the block.
But: only 3 deep defenders → vulnerable to powerful spikes in tight cross-courts.
Indication: youth teams, school, tactical opponents who play many tips or off-speed shots.
commonMistakes: Keeping the perimeter system against a team that tips → short balls lost.
Up-player too far forward (at the net) → blocked in his blocking momentum.
Libero who does not drop back → hole at the back on a powerful spike.
Confusing "W defense" and "man-up" in team vocabulary — source of misunderstandings.

6v6-defense-perimeter.title: Defense · perimeter (2-0-4)
6v6-defense-perimeter.shortDescription: White defense: 4 defenders on the lines, U open toward the net. Dominant in elite men's volleyball.

s1.title: 1. Perimeter configuration (2-0-4)
s1.description: The 4 defenders form a U open toward the net, almost on the lines — "one foot on the line" (Liskevych). The middle of the court is deliberately abandoned.

s2.title: 2. Opposing high set to Z4
s2.description: Set to their left wing. Our front line identifies the zone, the perimeter players stay strictly on the lines.

s3.title: 3. Double block + 4 defenders on the perimeter
s3.description: Standard double block (opposite line + middle cross-court). No defender pulled up behind the block (hence the 0 in the middle). Libero on the left line, P6 on the baseline, P1 on the right line.

s4.title: 4. Powerful line spike + block
s4.description: The hitter strikes the line on our back-left corner. The trajectory passes close to the block — a long block-out is likely.

s5.title: 5. Recovery on the line
s5.description: The libero recovers on the line — perfect perimeter coverage. Easily identifies "out" balls. High bump to zone 2-3.

s6.title: 6. RESET — perimeter
s6.description: Back to the pure perimeter formation: all backs on the lines, central middle abandoned by tactical convention.

keyPoints: Perimeter = 2-0-4 ("white defense"): 4 defenders on the perimeter, none pulled up.
System dominant in modern and international men's volleyball where power dominates.
Logic: statistically populate the zones where powerful spikes land (lines and deep corners).
Excellent identification of "out" balls and defense of block-outs.
⚠ The middle of the court (central zone between 3 and 5 m) is deliberately left open.
commonMistakes: Defenders collapsing toward the center → lose the system's logic and no longer cover the lines.
System chosen against a team that tips → center of the court uncovered, tips lost.
Inexperienced libero → misread of "out" balls on the sides.
Lack of athleticism to dive forward on tips → weakness exploited.

6v6-defense-read.title: Defense · read
6v6-defense-read.shortDescription: Elite reactive defense: adaptive positions based on set, approach and opposing armed-arm cues.

s1.title: 1. Neutral base position
s1.description: All defenders in read position, knees flexed, feet parallel. Mandatory visual sequence: "ball → setter → ball → hitter".

s2.title: 2. Read the set (toward opposing Z2)
s2.description: As soon as the ball leaves the opposing setter's hands → adjust toward the attack zone. Here opposing Z2 (their right = our left).

s3.title: 3. Read the hitter + adjustment
s3.description: Read in parallel the approach, the armed-arm orientation and shoulders. Everyone repositions based on the cues: high shoulder = spike, rotation = probable direction.

s4.title: 4. Read spike + double block
s4.description: The hitter opens long cross-court. Defense is already in place thanks to visual cues. OH + middle block. "Stopped on contact" mandatory.

s5.title: 5. Read recovery by the libero
s5.description: Perfect anticipation: the libero is already in the long cross-court, exactly on the trajectory. High bump to the target.

s6.title: 6. RESET — neutral base
s6.description: Back to neutral position, ready to read the next phase. The read restarts at every opposing touch.

keyPoints: Read defense = no fixed positioning, everything is adaptive. Modern defense is defined less by formation than by reading.
Visual sequence "ball → setter → ball → hitter" (Hebert, Liskevych, FIVB Top Volley).
Phases: neutral base → read set → read hitter → adjustment → "stopped on contact" → pursuit.
Preferred system at the international elite level (FIVB seniors).
Most effective against versatile hitters.
commonMistakes: Moving BEFORE the set → bad read, player on the wrong foot.
Incomplete read: only reading the set, not the armed arm.
Still moving at the moment of the hitter's contact (not "stopped on contact") → reactivity cut in half.
Lack of coordination → 2 defenders on the same ball, hole elsewhere.

6v6-defense-rotation.title: Defense · rotation (3-2-1)
6v6-defense-rotation.shortDescription: Rotation / slide defense: backs slide toward the attack side, the opposite back moves up behind the block.

s1.title: 1. Base + read of the Z4 set
s1.description: Base configuration before rotating. The opposing setter penetrates and prepares a set to their left wing.

s2.title: 2. High set to opposing Z4
s2.description: Standard distribution. Our team triggers the rotation: P1 will move up behind the block, P6 will slide toward the right line, libero keeps the cross-court.

s3.title: 3. 3-2-1 rotation engaged
s3.description: The setter (P1) MOVES UP to 3 m behind the block to cover the tip. P6 slides toward the right line at 8 m. Libero stays in the long cross-court. R4 classic off-blocker on the left.

s4.title: 4. Cross-court spike + block
s4.description: The hitter strikes long cross-court. Double block (opposite + middle) — the main trajectory is covered by the libero.

s5.title: 5. Libero defense on the cross-court
s5.description: The libero is exactly at the landing spot of the primary hit. High bump to zone 2-3 — smooth transition to counter-attack.

s6.title: 6. RESET — base before next rotation
s6.description: Back to base. The rotation was effective: the short tip would have been picked up by the up-setter, the long cross-court by the libero.

keyPoints: 3-2-1 rotation (slide defense): 3 back defenders slide toward the attack side.
The opposite back (often the setter if in P1) MOVES UP behind the block to cover the tip.
Back middle slides toward the line on the attacked side (~8.5 m, 1-1.5 m from the line).
Excellent coverage of the deep line AND tip simultaneously.
Quick setter transition if the setter is the up-player.
"Counter-rotate" variant: rotation in the opposite direction.
commonMistakes: Incomplete rotation → coverage holes.
Opposite-diagonal corner vulnerable (one less defender deep).
Confusion between rotate (toward the ball) and counter-rotate (opposite) — requires strong communication.
Up-player frozen → does not read tips vs spikes.

6v6-defense-vs-pipe.title: Defense · opposing pipe (BIC)
6v6-defense-vs-pipe.shortDescription: Defense against an opposing pipe (back-row Z6 attack): block-of-1 or 2, P6 moves up to "cinch the court".
6v6-defense-vs-pipe.contextLabel: 5-1 · Pipe / BIC · P6 up, tightened perimeter

s1.title: 1. Reading the pipe
s1.description: Their setter is about to send a flat set to the center back. Our middle scans both the possible opposing middle AND the pipe lane. P6 must be ready to move up.

s2.title: 2. Flat central set + pipe approach
s2.description: The opposing setter delivers a flat set toward the Z6 axis. The pipe hitter enters his approach from behind the 3 m line, long run-up. P6 starts sliding forward.

s3.title: 3. Central block + tightened wings
s3.description: Our middle alone jumps on the pipe. Wings (OH + opposite) drop to ~1.5 m from the net to cover lateral deflections. Z1 and Z5 sacrifice the lines to defend the axis.

s4.title: 4. Pipe hit + central block
s4.description: The hitter strikes deep on the axis. Our middle goes up to the net for a block-of-1 — the fast pipe doesn't allow time to put up two blockers.

s5.title: 5. Axial recovery by P6
s5.description: The ball crosses to the deep axis — P6 (pulled up to 6.5 m) is exactly on the impact spot. Bump straight on axis to the setter's zone 2-3.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to the tightened base
s6.description: Switch to the pipe-ready base position: P6 up, Z1/Z5 on the central axis. The configuration remains valid if play continues to rotate.

keyPoints: Pipe = back-row attack from Z6 (center back) by OH2 or OPP — targets the deep central axis.
Block-of-1 (middle) most frequent — double block hard on a fast tempo.
Defensive P6 MOVES UP to ~6-7 m from the net, exact axis ("cinch the court").
Z1 and Z5 close toward the center (~7 m, 1.5 m from the lines) — sacrifice the lines a bit.
BIC (fast pipe) = one of the hardest attacks to defend since the middle can't honor quick + pipe + two wings.
commonMistakes: Double block on a pipe → leaves a wing completely open if the opponent switches attacks.
P6 frozen at the back (8 m+) → fast pipe lands before he moves.
Z1/Z5 spread too wide on the lines → central axis uncovered.
No communication between middle and wings on who takes the pipe vs the quick.

6v6-defense-vs-z2.title: Defense · opposing Z2 attack
6v6-defense-vs-z2.shortDescription: Perfect mirror of Z4. Double block (OH line + middle cross-court) against opposing Z2 attack → arrives on our left.
6v6-defense-vs-z2.contextLabel: 5-1 · P1 back-row setter · Double block · Perimeter

s1.title: 1. Opposing reception + penetration
s1.description: Their back has bumped. The opposing setter penetrates from their P1 to the target. Our defense reads in READY.

s2.title: 2. Opposing high set to Z2
s2.description: The opposing setter distributes to their right wing. The attack arrives on our front-LEFT corner. Perfect mirror configuration of Z4.

s3.title: 3. Mirror double block + defensive shift
s3.description: OH (P4) blocker line + middle (P3) closes the cross-court. Opposite (P2) off-blocker on the right at the 3 m line. Libero defends the deep left line. P1 takes the long cross-court.

s4.title: 4. Opposing spike + double block
s4.description: The opposing right wing hits long cross-court. OH and middle jump. Stopped on contact mandatory.

s5.title: 5. Setter defense on the cross-court
s5.description: The setter (P1) is on the primary trajectory of the long cross-court. Defensive bump — immediate question: who takes the 2nd touch?

s6.title: 6. Opposite relay + counter-attack
s6.description: The opposite leaves his off-blocker spot to make the 2nd touch. Distribution to the OH in zone 4 who prepares the hit.

s7.title: 7. RESET — back to defensive base
s7.description: Everyone switches to base position as soon as the ball goes back to the opposing side.

keyPoints: Perfect mirror of Z4: OH (P4 = OH) blocker line + middle (P3) closes the cross-court.
The opposite (P2 = OPP) becomes off-blocker on the right side, drops off on the 3 m line.
The setter at P1 (back-row) defends the long cross-court.
Critical management: if the setter is in P2 (front-row), HE blocks the line — tense transition.
If the setter defends in P1 → 2nd touch by the opposite (back-up setter) is mandatory.
commonMistakes: Opposite blocking from zone 2 → off-blocker missing on the right side.
Middle not aligning with the OH → open block.
Libero misplaced on Z2 — defends the deep LINE here, not the long cross-court.
Setter defending AND wanting to relay → confusion on the 2nd touch.

6v6-defense-vs-z3.title: Defense · opposing Z3 attack (quick / tempo 1)
6v6-defense-vs-z3.shortDescription: Block-of-1 in read (middle) against opposing fast central attack — backs pulled up by one meter.

s1.title: 1. Opposing reception + lightning penetration
s1.description: Their back has just bumped. The setter sprints to the net for a quick. Tempo 1 = 0.3-0.5 s between set and hit. Our middle scans the opposing middle's movement, already on the move.

s2.title: 2. Flat set + middle airborne
s2.description: The opposing setter sends a very low flat set to the middle who has already taken off. Our wings drop to the 3 m line to free up block deflections.

s3.title: 3. Block-of-1 + fast spike
s3.description: Our middle alone jumps on read. The opposing middle hits short cross-court. The most dangerous shot: ball diving under the block.

s4.title: 4. Setter defense on the straight line
s4.description: Z1 (setter) and Z5 (libero) are pulled up to ~7 m since angles are short on a quick. The setter (Z1) recovers in his channel.

s5.title: 5. 2nd touch by the opposite (back-up setter)
s5.description: Since our setter has defended, the opposite at P2 takes the 2nd touch to relay. Our OH prepares a counter-attack in zone 4.

s6.title: 6. RESET — back to base
s6.description: Switch to base position as soon as the opposing setter touches the ball. Defense reorganizes for the next sequence.

keyPoints: Block-of-1 on the central quick: only the middle jumps (read most frequent, commit if scouting is strong).
Z1 and Z5 ADVANCE one meter (~7.5 m) since angles are shorter on a quick.
Wings stay on the 3 m line (~2-2.5 m from the net) for block deflections.
"Stopped on contact": everyone stopped and balanced at the exact moment of the hit.
commonMistakes: All front-row players jumping → leaves wings open for the next set.
Block too late → ball passes over the hands.
"False stepping" (first step backwards) → wasting the little time available.
Z1/Z5 frozen at the back (8 m+) → fast ball lands short before they've moved.

6v6-defense-vs-z4.title: Defense · opposing Z4 attack
6v6-defense-vs-z4.shortDescription: Double block on opposing zone-4 attack (their left wing → arrives on our right) in perimeter defense.
6v6-defense-vs-z4.contextLabel: 5-1 · P1 back-row setter · Double block · Perimeter

s1.title: 1. Opposing reception + penetration
s1.description: Their back has just bumped. The opposing setter penetrates toward his target between Z2 and Z3. Our defense reads in READY, visual sequence "ball → setter → ball → hitter".

s2.title: 2. Opposing high set to Z4
s2.description: The opposing setter distributes a lofted set to their left wing. The attack will arrive on our front-right corner. The front line already identifies the attack zone.

s3.title: 3. Double block + perimeter shift
s3.description: Opposite (P2) line + middle (P3) closes the cross-court. R4 off-blocker on the 3 m line on the left side. Libero in long cross-court ~7.5 m, P6 on axis at 8 m, P1 deep line in the block shadow.

s4.title: 4. Opposing spike + double block
s4.description: The opposing hitter strikes long cross-court. Opposite and middle jump in parallel. At the moment of contact, all defenders are stopped and balanced ("stopped on contact").

s5.title: 5. Libero defense on the long cross-court
s5.description: The libero is exactly on the primary trajectory (long cross-court). High bump to zone 2-3 to prepare the counter-attack.

s6.title: 6. Counter-attack by the OH
s6.description: Our setter delivers a high set to the OH who has dropped back to the 3 m line. Long cross-court hit on the opposing side to close the rally.

s7.title: 7. RESET — back to defensive base
s7.description: Everyone switches to base position as soon as the ball returns to the opposing side — no transition frozen in reception formation.

keyPoints: Double block: opposite (P2) line + middle (P3) cross-court. This is the FIVB standard configuration on opposing Z4.
Off-blocker = OH (P4) on the 3 m line on the left side — covers cut shot and short tip.
Perimeter system: libero (P5) in long cross-court ~7.5 m, P6 on axis ~8 m, P1 deep line in the block shadow.
Libero aligned with the inside shoulder of the central blocker — that's his priority zone.
Main shot defended: long cross-court (the opposing OH is the most solicited).
commonMistakes: Unintentionally open block (P3 not aligned with P2) → ball passes between the blockers.
Off-blocker staying at the net → block shadow uncovered (mistake #1 according to Hebert).
Misplaced libero (too close to the net) → deep spikes land.
Setter who blocks then doesn't get to the net → 2nd touch by a non-specialized player.
Defenders still moving at the moment of the hitter's contact (not "stopped on contact").

4v4-reception-losange.title: 4v4 · Diamond reception
4v4-reception-losange.shortDescription: Canonical diamond formation: setter at P3 (center net) + 2 wings on the 3 m line + back deep.

s1.title: 1. Diamond formation
s1.description: Canonical 1-2-1 layout: setter AT THE CENTER of the net (P3), 2 wings on the 3 m line (L + R), back deep. No libero allowed in 4v4 school. Everyone READY.

s2.title: 2. Serve + back bump
s2.description: Lofted serve to the central zone. The lone back calls "Mine!" and steps slightly toward the ball.

s3.title: 3. Set to the left wing
s3.description: High bump to the setter at the center of the net (no penetration in the diamond). He distributes to zone 4. The left wing chains his short approach.

s4.title: 4. Ball available + short coverage
s4.description: The set arrives in zone 4. The right wing tightens toward the center to cover, the back moves up slightly. With a single opposing block, the hitting angle stays wide.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to the diamond
s5.description: Everyone resumes their position in the diamond for the next serve.

keyPoints: Canonical diamond (1-2-1) = the most used 4v4 formation.
"Center setter" variant: setter at P3 at the net, distributes left OR right.
No libero allowed in 4v4 school — everyone must know how to receive.
Each player covers ~30-40 m² (vs ~20 m² in 6v6).
commonMistakes: Confusion on central balls between 2 zones → call mandatory.
Lone back too far back → short balls behind the net not covered.
Setter who also receives → impossible to make the 2nd touch behind.

4v4-reception-u.title: 4v4 · U-formation reception
4v4-reception-u.shortDescription: U formation: setter out + 3 receivers (left, back, right).

s1.title: 1. U configuration
s1.description: The setter is hidden at P2 at the net. 3 receivers in a U: left wing, back center, right wing. Each player covers about 1/3 of the width.

s2.title: 2. Serve + left wing bump
s2.description: Lofted serve to the left channel. The left wing calls and takes the ball in his channel. High trajectory to give the setter time.

s3.title: 3. Distribution to the left wing
s3.description: The ball arrives at the fixed setter in zone 2 (no penetration in 4v4). Quick distribution to the left wing who immediately chains his approach.

s4.title: 4. Ball available in zone 4
s4.description: The set arrives in zone 4 for the left wing. System more offensive than the diamond: the setter has not received, the attack is fast and readable.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to the U
s5.description: The 3 receivers return to the U and the setter goes back to his hiding spot at P2.

keyPoints: U reception = the most effective competitive 4v4 configuration.
3 specialized receivers + setter out = 1 player available for the attack without having received.
Target: zone 2 (fixed setter) → fast distribution.
Technically more demanding than the diamond but more offensive.
commonMistakes: Wing not covering the whole channel → ball between wing and back lost.
Back center too far forward → long balls pass overhead.
Setter leaning toward reception → confusion.

5-1-reception-3-receivers.title: Reception · 3-receiver (5-1)
5-1-reception-3-receivers.shortDescription: 3-receiver reception (libero + 2 OHs) with setter out and opposite hidden — modern standard formation.

s1.title: 1. Reception position
s1.description: Three receivers in an arc: left OH, central libero, right OH. Each covers ~1/3 of the width. The setter and opposite hide at the net, ready to step in as soon as the server hits.

s2.title: 2. Serve + bump
s2.description: Lofted serve to the left OH who calls "Mine!" and bumps. In parallel, the setter triggers his penetration from his hiding spot at P1 toward zone 2-3.

s3.title: 3. High set to zone 4
s3.description: The ball rises to the target (between P2 and P3) where the setter arrives just in time. He distributes a lofted set to zone 4. The receiving OH has already triggered his drop back to the 3 m line.

s4.title: 4. Ball available to the hitter
s4.description: The ball arrives in zone 4 at hitting height. The OH takes his last steps before his jump. The quality of the set validates the quality of the initial reception.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to formation
s5.description: The whole team resumes its reception position for the next serve.

keyPoints: 3-receiver reception = modern 5-1 standard. Maximum specialization.
Target: zone 2-3, one arm from the net, height ~3 m.
The setter stays hidden at the net until the server hits, then penetrates.
The receiving OH IMMEDIATELY chains his attack approach.
commonMistakes: Reception too flat or too short → setter arrives late.
Conflict between 2 receivers → vocal call mandatory.
OH frozen after reception → loses an offensive option in zone 4.

5v5-reception-4-receivers.title: 5v5 · 4-receiver reception
5v5-reception-4-receivers.shortDescription: 5v5 format: setter out + 4 receivers in U or in line.

s1.title: 1. 5v5 configuration
s1.description: The setter (at P2) is out at the net. The 4 receivers form a U: 2 on the 3 m line, 2 deep. The best receiver takes the most exposed zone.

s2.title: 2. Serve + back bump
s2.description: Lofted serve in the back-left channel. The left back calls and bumps in his channel.

s3.title: 3. Set to zone 4
s3.description: The ball arrives at the fixed setter in zone 2 (no penetration in 5v5). Quick distribution to the left wing. The front-left starts his approach.

s4.title: 4. Ball available — 3-player coverage
s4.description: The set arrives in zone 4. The front-left takes his steps. Coverage in 5v5 is done with only 3 players (not 5 as in 6v6) — the middle and setter stay close.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to the U
s5.description: The 4 receivers find their place in the U, setter fixed at P2.

keyPoints: In 5v5 without a libero, the best receiver takes the most exposed zone.
U formation: 2 receivers on the 3 m line + 2 deep.
In-line variant possible (4 lined up at mid-court) if levels are similar.
No penetration → fixed setter (simplified 4-1 system).
commonMistakes: U shape too narrow → long cross-courts uncovered.
Weak receiver → isolate them in the smallest zone.
Setter who still penetrates → confusion with standard 6v6.

5v5-reception-pentagon.title: 5v5 · Pentagon reception
5v5-reception-pentagon.shortDescription: Pentagon reception (5 players without a setter out) — beginner or recreational version.

s1.title: 1. 5-player pentagon
s1.description: All players receive. No dedicated setter — whoever touches first leaves the 2nd touch to the player closest to the net. Recreational / beginner configuration.

s2.title: 2. Serve + center calls
s2.description: Serve to the central medium zone. The center player calls and bumps — that's his area in the pentagon.

s3.title: 3. Opportunity set
s3.description: The ball rises toward the center of the net. The front-right, closest to the ball, steps forward and takes the 2nd touch with a high set depending on the quality of the reception.

s4.title: 4. Ball available — simple system
s4.description: The set goes to the front-left. Readable distribution, ideal for beginners. Any player can make the 2nd touch depending on the ball's angle.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to pentagon
s5.description: The 5 players find their place in the pentagon for the next serve.

keyPoints: Pentagon without a dedicated setter = recreational or beginner configuration.
5 players in a pentagon: 2 in front, 1 center, 2 in the back.
Any player can make the 2nd touch depending on where the ball arrives.
Advantage: great adaptability. Drawback: less offensive consistency.
commonMistakes: No hierarchy on the 2nd touch → 2 players hesitate.
Center frozen → balls on each side missed.
Systematic high sets without clear distribution.

6v6-reception-2-receivers.title: Reception · 2-receiver (elite)
6v6-reception-2-receivers.shortDescription: Ultra-specialized 2-receiver reception (libero + OH): all others ready to attack.

s1.title: 1. 2-receiver configuration
s1.description: Only 2 receivers: libero on the left side, receiving OH on the right side. The 4 other players are already in attack stance, ready to trigger as soon as the serve is struck.

s2.title: 2. Serve + libero bump
s2.description: Serve to the left. The libero calls and bumps. With only 2 zones, the technical demand is extreme: an exceptional libero is required. The setter triggers his penetration.

s3.title: 3. Set + simultaneous approaches
s3.description: The ball rises to the target. The setter distributes to zone 4. The attacking OH, free of any reception, launches a fast approach at full speed — he arrives at full power.

s4.title: 4. Ball available — maximum variety
s4.description: The ball arrives in zone 4 for the attacking OH. At that moment the setter simultaneously has a middle on quick and an opposite on a back-row attack available — 3-hitter combinations possible.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to 2-receiver formation
s5.description: The libero and the receiving OH return to their zones, the hitters reposition ready to attack.

keyPoints: 2-receiver reception = elite configuration (professional volleyball).
Used on easy serves or "front-row setter" rotations.
Maximum offensive variety: all hitters available immediately.
Extreme technical demand: 2 solid receivers required.
commonMistakes: Adopting this system against a powerful serve → catastrophic receptions.
Attacking OH not starting his approach in parallel → option lost.
No call → hesitation between the 2 receivers.

6v6-reception-4-2.title: Reception · 4-2 (4 receivers)
6v6-reception-4-2.shortDescription: 4-2 system: fixed setter at P2 + 4 receivers (the 2 OHs + middle + back).

s1.title: 1. 4-2 layout
s1.description: 4-2 system: 2 opposing setters. The front setter (P2) and the front middle step out at the net. 4 receivers in a trapezoid: 2 OHs on the diagonal, back middle and back setter deep.

s2.title: 2. Serve + left OH bump
s2.description: Lofted serve to the left channel. The left OH calls and bumps. The setter is already fixed at P2 at the net, no penetration.

s3.title: 3. Set to the left wing
s3.description: The ball arrives at the fixed setter at P2 (easy target, no movement). He distributes to the left wing. The left OH immediately chains his approach.

s4.title: 4. Ball available in zone 4
s4.description: The set is in place. In 4-2, only 2 offensive options exist in front (the middle and the wing) → readable but limited distribution.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to trapezoid
s5.description: The whole team resumes its position in the 4-2 system.

keyPoints: 4-receiver reception = 4-2 system. 2 front-row players out (setter + front middle).
Bigger zones than in a W but less demanding than a 3-receiver reception.
Easy target: the setter does not move.
Drawback: only 2 hitters in front.
commonMistakes: Front middle who also receives → no commit at the net.
Trapezoid too open → central balls not covered.
Confusion on the 2nd touch between the 2 setters.

6v6-reception-rotation-p4.title: Reception · 5-1 P4 rotation
6v6-reception-rotation-p4.shortDescription: P4 special case: the setter and the middle shift left to free the OH in zone 6.

s1.title: 1. Left shift
s1.description: BEFORE the hit: the setter (P4) and the middle (P3) place themselves AS FAR LEFT as alignment rules allow. This shift frees zone 6 for the receiving OH.

s2.title: 2. Serve + bump by the OH in P6
s2.description: Serve to the central zone 6. The OH in P6 calls and bumps in the zone freed by the setter's shift. Three receivers: libero, OH and opposite (on the edge).

s3.title: 3. Penetration + OH* switch
s3.description: The setter rushes from P4 to zone 2-3. Simultaneously, the OH* in P2 crosses over to P4 to attack. The middle repositions in zone 3.

s4.title: 4. Ball available for OH* in zone 4
s4.description: The set arrives for the OH* who has completed his crossover. With only 2 hitters in front (OH* + middle), the main option is the left wing.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to the shift
s5.description: All players resume the left shift for the next serve in P4 rotation.

keyPoints: In P4, the setter and middle MUST shift left at the serve.
This shift opens zone 6 for the OH reception at P6.
Setter↔OH* switch mandatory during the set.
The opposite (in P1) does not receive and stays ready for a back-row attack.
commonMistakes: Shift forgotten → reception conflict in zone 6.
Switch too late → OH* attacks at P2 (wrong side).
Opposite who receives → loses the back-row attack option.

6v6-reception-semi-circle.title: Reception · semi-circle
6v6-reception-semi-circle.shortDescription: Reception in an arc open toward the server, equidistant. U15-U18 stage.

s1.title: 1. Semi-circular arc
s1.description: The 5 receivers form an arc equidistant from the server. All oriented toward the setter hidden at P1. The middle stays in reception (vs out in the 3-receiver formation).

s2.title: 2. Serve + common read
s2.description: Lofted serve to the central zone. All players read in the same direction. The middle calls his ball — it's his zone in the arc.

s3.title: 3. Penetration + high set
s3.description: The setter leaves his hiding spot as the ball rises. He arrives at the target in zone 2-3 and distributes to the left wing where the left OH has already started his approach.

s4.title: 4. Ball available in zone 4
s4.description: The set arrives in zone 4. The left OH is in position to hit. Classic, readable distribution — typical of the U15-U18 learning stage.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to the arc
s5.description: Everyone returns to the semi-circular arc for the next serve.

keyPoints: Semi-circular arc = intermediate stage between W and 3-receiver reception.
The 5 players equidistant from the server → homogeneous coverage.
Suited to youth teams (U15-U18) learning specialization.
Keeps a middle in reception (vs 3-receiver where he is out).
commonMistakes: Arc too open to the sides → holes in the center.
Players too far from the server → late reaction to fast serves.
Conflict with the setter who also wants to receive.

6v6-reception-w.title: Reception · W (5 receivers)
6v6-reception-w.shortDescription: W formation: 5 players except the setter. Suited to beginners and the 4-2 system.

s1.title: 1. W formation
s1.description: W layout: 2 front players at mid-court, 1 middle player in the center, 2 backs deep. The setter is already out at the net at P2 (4-2 system). Each player defends a small, well-defined zone.

s2.title: 2. Serve + middle player calls
s2.description: Lofted serve to the central zone. The middle player calls "Mine!" because the ball lands in the central pocket of the W, equidistant from the front players.

s3.title: 3. High set to zone 4
s3.description: Bump aimed at zone 2 where the setter already waits at the net (no penetration in 4-2). He distributes a lofted set to zone 4. The front-left triggers his approach.

s4.title: 4. Ball available to the hitter
s4.description: The ball arrives in zone 4. The front-left takes his last steps. In 4-2, offensive options are limited (2 hitters in front), but the simplicity of the system compensates.

s5.title: 5. RESET — back to W formation
s5.description: Everyone returns to their zone in the W for the next serve.

keyPoints: W formation = 5 receivers, the setter steps out.
Small individual zones → less doubt, few conflicts.
Ideal in U13/U15 and in the 4-2 system (beginners).
Drawback: specialized hitters are constrained in reception.
commonMistakes: Central conflict between middle player and front players → call mandatory.
Players too frozen in their zone → ball between 2 zones lost.
Setter staying in reception → impossible to make the 2nd touch.
